newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian organised crime tightening grip - minister.
newsitem.headline: Russian organised crime tightening grip - minister.

text.p: Mafia-style gangs are tightening their grip over Russia's economy and political and judicial systems, imperilling the country's security and market reforms, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said on Friday.
He told a meeting of senior government ministers that Russia urgently needed a nationwide strategy to combat organised crime, whose tentacles reached into the highest levels of power.

"On the broadest possible level, organised crime is infiltrating different organs of state power and the forces of law and order, including the police and the judicial system," Kulikov told reporters after the meeting.

The number of registered crimes by organised groups has jumped by 94 percent over the past five years. There are more than 9,000 such groups now operating in Russia, employing around 100,000 people, the interior ministry said in a statement.

The country's lack of an effective legal base, weak government safeguards and rampant corruption have all contributed to the growth of organised crime as Russia has moved towards a market economy, it said.

"We have not achieved any meaningful breakthrough in the battle with organised crime. Organised criminal groupings have effectively preserved their positions in the most profitable branches of the economy," the statement said.
Earlier this year President Boris Yeltsin accused mafia "godfathers" of hijacking his economic reforms, and launched a high-profile campaign against graft.

Kulikov, a four-star general who appeared at the briefing in his trademark khaki uniform complete with medal ribbons, said Yeltsin's strong personal interest in the issue had given new impetus to the fight against organised crime.
"By his uncompromising stance the president has created a good moral climate (in the anti-corruption drive). Our hands are not tied," said Kulikov.
He added that the ministers at Friday's meeting had unanimously agreed to make the fight against organised crime a top political priority.

Kulikov said one key requirement was greater coordination between the different law-enforcement bodies, which include his ministry, the prosecutor's office and the Federal Security Service, successor organisation to the Soviet-era KGB.

Organised criminal groupings are particularly active in the highly lucrative energy, gold and diamond sectors as well as in such traditional areas as the arms trade, drug trafficking and alcohol and tobacco production, the ministry said.
It put the current value of Russia's illegal drugs trade at around $7 billion, 650 times greater than in 1991. The world's total illegal drugs trade is estimated at $500 billion.

Kulikov noted a sharp growth in terrorism by the criminal gangs. In 1996 Russia recorded 886 explosions, up from just 18 in 1994 as bombs became a popular method of settling scores between gangs in their ongoing turf battles.

Registered organised crimes in 1996 totalled nearly 21,000, an increase of six percent from the previous year. Court cases had been initiated against nearly half of these crimes, many of which involved extortion and blackmail.
Kulikov said he hoped that Russia's planned spending cuts -- made necessary by a big shortfall in revenue due to widespread tax evasion -- would not undermine the fight against crime.

Underlining Russia's lawless image, U.S. tobacco group Philip Morris Companies Inc announced on Friday it had evacuated two Moscow-based British staff and their families after they received threats. It gave no details about the threats.
Asked about the incident, Kulikov said his ministry was examining ways of improving security for Russian and foreign businessmen.
Threats and murders of Russian businessmen have become commonplace in the wild atmosphere of post-Soviet capitalism, although incidents involving Western businessmen are still relatively rare.
